---
title: "4. Cross-validation and model comparison"
description: >
  Which model predicts held-out surveys best, and are its intervals
  calibrated? Random and spatial cross-validation, and comparing models on
  the same folds.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
```

`diagnose()` says whether the sampler has found the posterior. It does not
say whether the model is any good. Cross-validation asks a sharper question:
how well does a model predict surveys it has not seen? This tutorial uses
the crt K76T data of [tutorial 1](crt76t.html) to show how to:

- check that a model's predictive intervals are calibrated;
- compare models on the same held-out data, with an honest standard error;
- hold out whole countries, to test extrapolation rather than
  interpolation.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. How `crossval()` works

`crossval()` splits the observed area-time cells into folds. It holds out
each fold in turn, refits the model to the rest, and predicts the
held-out cells. Each prediction is scored against the surveys:

- **log score**: the log probability the model gave to the observed count.
  It is higher for better models, and is the main basis for comparison.
- **outside the 95% interval**: about 5% for a calibrated model. The check
  uses a randomised PIT (probability integral transform), so 5% is the right
  target whatever the number tested.
- **RMSE** and **correlation** of the predicted against the observed
  prevalence: easy to read, but blind to the intervals.

Each fold is a full refit, so 10-fold cross-validation costs 10 fits. The
refits can be shorter than a publication run: they only need to pass
`diagnose()`. Tutorial 1's pilot passed it at 3,000 iterations, and the
refits here use 6,000.

Why not leave-one-out on the fitted model (PSIS-LOO, as in the `loo`
package)? With one latent value per observed cell, each cell's posterior
leans heavily on its own data, and the importance weights become unstable.
Refitting is slower, but it is reliable.

## 2. Three models, one set of folds

```{r data}
fr <- areal_frame(igad_adm1, id = "id", groups = c(country = "country"),
                  link_within = "country", adjacency_snap = 2000, verbose = FALSE)
tf <- time_frame(1989, 2024, "year")
d <- areal_data(igad_crt76t, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day", verbose = FALSE)
```

The default model of tutorial 1, and two simpler ones: without the cell
nugget, and without the trend.

```{r fit-cv, eval = FALSE}
ctl <- list(n_iter = 6000, n_burn = 2000, n_store = 250, theta_thin = 4)
models <- list(
  default   = fit_areal(d, control = ctl),
  no_nugget = fit_areal(d, nugget = FALSE, control = ctl),
  no_trend  = fit_areal(d, formula = ~ 1, control = ctl)
)
cv <- lapply(models, crossval, folds = 10, seed = 1)
```

The same `seed` gives the same random folds for every model, so all three
are scored on exactly the same held-out cells. Ten folds of three models is
thirty refits, and the country folds of section 5 add seven more: about
half an hour here, with each refit's chains in parallel. For longer jobs,
`fold =` runs some of the folds (e.g. in separate sessions), and
`checkpoint_dir` lets an interrupted refit resume.

```{r load, include = FALSE}
cache <- readRDS("_cache/crossval.rds")
cv <- cache$cv
cv_country <- cache$cv_country
cov <- readRDS("_cache/covariates.rds")$cv
```

```{r cv-print}
cv$default
head(cv$default$cells[, c("fold", "id", "time", "y", "k", "obs_prev", "pred_mean", "pred_lo", "pred_hi",
                          "log_score")])
```

## 3. Is the model calibrated?

If the predictive distributions are right, the PIT values are uniform: a
flat histogram, with about 5% of the surveys outside their 95% interval.

```{r pit, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(cv$default$cells, aes(pit)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1), fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = nrow(cv$default$cells) / 10, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "PIT", y = "held-out cells") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Predicted against observed prevalence, with each survey's 95% predictive
interval. That interval is for the survey's observed prevalence, so it
includes the binomial noise of its sample size, and it is what "outside"
refers to:

```{r obs-pred, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(cv$default$cells, aes(obs_prev, pred_mean, ymin = rep_lo, ymax = rep_hi, colour = outside)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey40", `TRUE` = "red")) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "observed prevalence (held out)", y = "predicted", colour = "outside the\n95% interval") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The histogram is close to flat, and `r sum(cv$default$cells$outside)` of
the `r nrow(cv$default$cells)` held-out cells are outside their 95%
interval, `r sum(cv$default$cells$pit < 0.025)` below and
`r sum(cv$default$cells$pit > 0.975)` above. Out of sample, the default
model is calibrated. The misses are surveys that disagree with their
neighbours, such as 0 of 103 positive in a Ugandan district where the
model expected about 4%, or 2 of 2 positive in Kenya in 2021, where it
expected 3%:

```{r misses}
subset(cv$default$cells, outside, c(id, time, y, k, obs_prev, pred_mean, rep_lo, rep_hi, pit))
```

## 4. Comparing models

`compare_cv()` lines the models up cell by cell. Most of the variation in
log score is between cells (some surveys are hard to predict for any
model), and comparing cell by cell removes it. `diff` is each model's mean
log score minus the best model's, and `se_diff` its standard error. A
difference of less than about two standard errors is not a clear
preference.

The covariate models of [tutorial 3](covariates.html) were
cross-validated with the same folds and refit length, so they join the
comparison:

```{r compare}
compare_cv(default = cv$default, no_nugget = cv$no_nugget, no_trend = cv$no_trend,
           smooth_trend = cov$smooth, kenya_uganda = cov$ku)
```

On log score, the five models are within about two standard errors of
each other. These data cannot tell them apart on held-out surveys. Two
things still stand out:

- **Without the nugget, `r round(cv$no_nugget$overall$pct_outside_95)`% of
  surveys fall outside their intervals.** The model must then explain
  every difference between surveys with the smooth field, and it becomes
  overconfident. The nugget earns its place through calibration, more
  than through the mean log score.
- **The covariate models predict held-out surveys no better, within the
  noise.** Yet tutorial 3 showed them changing the map in Ethiopia and
  Sudan after 2015. Random folds score surveyed area-years, where the
  data decide whatever the mean. Where there are no surveys, which is where the mean
  matters most, they are silent.

Keep the default unless there is a reason to prefer another. Section 5
looks at the places random folds cannot see.

## 5. Spatial cross-validation: holding out whole countries

Random folds hold out scattered cells, and their neighbours in space and
time usually stay in. They test **interpolation**. To ask how well the model
**extrapolates** to a country with no data, give `folds` a label for each
observed cell, here its country:

```{r country-folds, eval = FALSE}
country <- fr$groups$country[d$cells$area]
cv_country <- crossval(models$default, folds = country, seed = 1)
```

```{r country-results}
cv_country$folds[, c("fold", "n_held", "pct_outside_95", "mean_log_score", "rmse")]
```

Held out one country at a time, the model does worse on every measure:

```{r spatial-vs-random}
rbind(random = cv$default$overall, by_country = cv_country$overall)
```

Twice the target share of surveys fall outside their intervals. Most of
the misses are in Uganda and Ethiopia. Without its own surveys, Uganda is
predicted from Kenya and the rest, and its decline came later than
Kenya's. A Ugandan district with 1,664 of 1,729 positive in 2012 was
predicted at about 40%. A likely reason: the field's variance is learnt
mostly from differences between neighbouring units and years. Differences
between whole countries can be larger, and the model does not know it.

So where a whole country lacks surveys, treat the map's intervals as
optimistic.

`compare_cv()` compares models on the same folds, and refuses folds that
differ. Setting one model's random and spatial scores side by side, as
above, asks a different question: how much harder is extrapolation than
interpolation? Use random folds to choose between models for the map as a
whole, and spatial folds to judge how far to trust it where there are no
surveys.
